draft.title: Judging how a study was run
card: A study usually asks or tests a sample, not everyone. A fair sample is chosen at random, so each member of the group has a chance of being picked. A sample made of volunteers or of people who are easy to reach may not match the whole group.
When a study tests a treatment, a control group does not get it. Comparing the two groups shows whether the treatment made the difference, or whether the change would have happened anyway.
A small sample can give a result by luck. A larger sample, chosen fairly, is usually a better guide to the whole group.
Example: a gym says 9 out of 10 of its members feel fitter. Ask who was asked, whether any group did not train, and how many people took part.
draft.remember: Before you trust a study, check how the sample was chosen, whether there was a control group, and how big the sample was.

a.q: A school tests a new study app on 40 students. Another 40 students do not use it. Both groups sit the same test. What is the second group called?
a.why: The second group does not get the app, so it is the control group. Comparing the two test results shows whether the app made a difference. A random sample is about how people are picked, not about who gets the treatment.
a.clue: Which group does not get the treatment?

b.q: A café in Bendigo asks the first 12 customers through its door on a Monday morning if they like its new coffee. Nine say yes. The café says most people in town like the coffee. Which is the best criticism of this claim?
opts: The sample is small and not chosen at random
The sample has no control group to compare
Nine out of 12 is too few people saying yes
The café should have asked customers on Friday
b.why: Twelve customers is a small sample, and the first customers on a Monday are not a random pick of the town. They may not match the whole group. A control group is for testing a treatment, so it does not apply here.
b.clue: Think about who was asked and how many.

b.best: The sample is small and not chosen at random
